opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is going to be more dynamic than people assume, and the boundary between the two keeps moving.

Right now, a lot of agent products are built on top of a model's capabilities, so the model is really the foundation. When the model gets a big jump in ability, say in long-horizon reasoning, tool use, or coding, a whole layer of product engineering that people built to compensate for weaknesses suddenly becomes unnecessary. Things like complicated workflows, hand-written prompts chained together, or a lot of scaffolding can be absorbed into the model itself. So if your product's value is mainly about patching what the model can't yet do, that value is fragile. The next generation of models may just eat it.

But I don't think that means model companies will do everything. The model is getting more general, but the real world is very specific. There are lots of domains where the hard part isn't intelligence. It's the context: the data, the integration with existing systems, the trust of the users, and understanding what the job actually looks like day to day. Companies that are close to those scenarios, and that accumulate real feedback and real environments, have something the model company doesn't automatically have.

For us as a model company, I think the most important thing is to keep pushing the frontier of intelligence. That's where the leverage is. Agents are actually a very natural direction for the model itself, because in the end you want the model to take actions, use tools, and finish tasks end to end, not just answer questions. So we think about agentic capability as part of the model, not as a separate product layer. Training on real tasks and in real environments feeds back into making the model better. That loop between model and product is very important, so we'll definitely build some first-party agent products ourselves.

At the same time, an open ecosystem matters a lot. No single company can cover all the scenarios. If the model is strong and accessible, many teams can build on it, and what they learn also tells us what the model should be good at next. So it's partly competition and partly symbiosis.

If I had to summarize: in the short term it's complementary, in the medium term the overlap grows, and in the long term the winners on the application side will be the ones whose advantage gets stronger as models get better, not weaker. That's the question I'd ask any agent company: when the next model comes out, does your product get better, or does it become unnecessary?

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions in the industry right now, and honestly I don't think anyone has a settled answer. But let me share how I think about it.

In the short term, there's clearly a division of labor. Model companies produce intelligence, and application companies package that intelligence into something a user actually wants to use. That looks a lot like the cloud era, where infrastructure and application layers were separate businesses. A lot of people assume it will stay that way.

But I'm not sure that analogy holds. The key difference is that with cloud, the infrastructure didn't get better at doing the application's job. A database doesn't learn to become your SaaS product. A model does. Every generation of models absorbs capabilities that used to require careful engineering on top. Things like tool use, planning, long-horizon memory, self-correction. Two years ago those were things an agent company built with prompts and scaffolding. Now a lot of it lives inside the model itself. So the boundary keeps moving, and it moves in one direction.

That's why I believe the model and the agent will converge over time. The agent is not a wrapper around the model. The agent is what the model becomes when you train it end to end on real tasks with real environments and real feedback. If you accept that, then the most important agent products will be built by whoever controls training, because the product improvements flow from the training loop rather than from the engineering on top.

That doesn't mean application companies disappear. There's a huge amount of value in distribution, in domain data, in understanding a specific workflow deeply, in trust with a particular customer base. Those things are hard for a model company to replicate. And for many vertical scenarios, the economics simply don't justify a frontier lab paying attention. So I expect many very successful companies there.

But I'd say to anyone building an agent company: ask yourself whether your advantage is something the next model release can erase. If your whole moat is that the model is currently bad at X and you've patched around it, that's a very uncomfortable position. If your moat is a proprietary environment, proprietary feedback signal, or a relationship with users that generates data no one else has, then you're in a much better place, and you might even be the one who ends up doing the training eventually.

So the long-term relationship, I think, is less "supplier and customer" and more a competition over who owns the loop between the model and the world. The companies that close that loop, whether they started as a lab or as a product, are the ones that will matter.

astra-6.text:
I think in the long term, the boundary between model companies and agent companies will become less clear. If you want to build a really good agent, you’ll often need to improve the model itself. And if you want to improve a model, you need to understand how it performs on real tasks, with feedback from users. So there’s a strong reason for those two layers to move closer together.

But that doesn’t mean model companies will build every application. An agent company can have a much deeper understanding of a particular workflow, access to relevant data, and a close relationship with customers. Those things matter a lot. The question is whether you have a feedback loop that lets your product keep improving, rather than just an interface around a model that everyone else can also use.

So I’d expect both cooperation and competition. Model companies will build some agents, and agent companies will increasingly participate in training or adapting models. Where the boundary settles will depend on the task and on who can deliver the best result for the user.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, in the long run, there will be both cooperation and competition. Model companies will keep expanding what the underlying model can do, and some capabilities that today require a separate agent framework may become part of the model itself. So the boundary will keep moving.

For companies building agent products, the key question is what value they create as models improve. If the product is mainly a thin layer around a model, that can be difficult to sustain. But understanding a particular workflow, integrating with a customer’s systems, and making the product reliable enough for daily use—that is substantial work. A better model can make that business more valuable.

Model companies also have to choose where to focus. Building a general capability and delivering a complete product for a specific industry require different kinds of effort. So I don’t think one side necessarily absorbs the other. There will be overlap, but also room for a division of labor. The strongest relationships will be ones where improvements in the model translate directly into better outcomes for the agent’s users.
